units.title: Hello, Ada!
units.summary: Write your first Ada program and print text and numbers with Put_Line, Put and New_Line.

lesson.md: Ada is a programming language for software that must be reliable, for example in planes and trains. An Ada program is a **procedure**: a named list of steps. Here is a complete program that prints one line.

Line by line: `with Ada.Text_IO;` makes the package `Ada.Text_IO` available. It contains the tools for text input and output. `use Ada.Text_IO;` lets you write `Put_Line` instead of the long name `Ada.Text_IO.Put_Line`. `procedure Main is` starts the program called `Main`. The steps (statements) go between `begin` and `end Main;`. Every statement ends with a semicolon `;`.

`Put_Line` prints a text and then ends the line. `Put` prints a text and stays on the same line. `New_Line` ends the current line. If the line is empty, you get an empty line. A text (a **string**) goes in double quotes.
The operator `&` joins two strings into one longer string. You can join as many parts as you like.

Ada can calculate: `+` adds, `-` subtracts and `*` multiplies. But `Put_Line` only prints strings. `Integer'Image (5)` turns the whole number `5` into the string `" 5"`. The apostrophe `'` asks for an **attribute**, a property of a type. A positive number gets a space in front, where a negative number has its minus sign.

Ada does not care about upper and lower case in names: `PUT_LINE` and `Put_Line` are the same. The usual style is a capital letter at the start of each word, with `_` between words. A line that starts with `--` is a **comment**, and Ada ignores it.
`Put_Line (5);` does not compile. Ada never turns a number into a string by itself. Write `Put_Line (Integer'Image (5));` instead.

card: `with Ada.Text_IO; use Ada.Text_IO;` loads the text tools
`procedure Main is begin ... end Main;` is the program
`Put_Line ("Hi");` prints a line, `Put` stays on it, `New_Line` ends it
`"a" & "b"` joins strings, `Integer'Image (5)` gives `" 5"`

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Store values in variables, meet Integer, Float, Boolean and String, and see why Ada never mixes types.

lesson.md: A **variable** is a named place for a value. In Ada, you declare variables between `is` and `begin`. A declaration has the name, a colon `:`, the type and, if you like, `:=` with a first value.

`:=` gives a variable a new value. `Age := Age + 1;` takes the old value, adds `1` and stores the result. The single `=` does not assign in Ada. It compares two values, as you will see in the next unit.

Every variable has a **type** that decides what it can hold. `Integer` holds whole numbers, `Float` holds numbers with a decimal point, `Boolean` holds `True` or `False`, and `String` holds text. Each type has its own `'Image` attribute.

`Float'Image` uses scientific notation: `2.50000E+00` means 2.5 times 10 to the power 0. `Boolean'Image` writes the value in capitals. With two integers, `/` divides and drops the remainder, `mod` gives the remainder, and `**` raises to a power.

Ada never mixes types by itself. `Count * Price` with an `Integer` and a `Float` does not compile. You convert a value with the name of the target type: `Float (Count)`. `Integer (4.5)` rounds to the nearest whole number, and a value exactly in the middle goes away from zero, so it gives `5`.
A **constant** is declared with the word `constant`. It gets its value once and can never change. A statement that assigns to a constant does not compile.
An Ada `String` has a fixed length. `Name : String := "Ada";` has exactly 3 characters forever. `Name := "Grace";` stops the program with `Constraint_Error`, because 5 characters do not fit into 3.

card: `X : Integer := 5;` declares a variable before `begin`
`X := X + 1;` assigns a new value
`Integer`, `Float`, `Boolean`, `String` are basic types
`Float (N)` converts, Ada never mixes types by itself
`Max : constant Integer := 9;` can never change

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Let your program choose with if, elsif and else, combine conditions with and then, and pick a branch with case.

lesson.md: An `if` statement runs code only when a condition is `True`. It has the form `if condition then`, the statements, and `end if;`. To compare values you use `=` (equal), `/=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`.

`else` gives the statements for the case when the condition is `False`. `elsif` checks another condition. Ada checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first branch whose condition is `True`. Note the spelling: `elsif`, not `else if`.

`and` is `True` when both sides are `True`, `or` when at least one side is `True`, and `not` turns `True` into `False`. With `and then`, Ada checks the right side only when the left side is `True`. With `or else`, only when the left side is `False`. Here `and then` protects the program from a division by zero.

A `case` statement picks a branch by the value of a variable. Each branch starts with `when` and `=>`. `|` means "or", `1 .. 5` means all values from 1 to 5, and `when others` covers every value not listed yet. Ada requires that every possible value is covered.
`=` compares and `:=` assigns. `if X := 5 then` does not compile. A `case` on an `Integer` without `when others` does not compile either, because it cannot list every whole number.
Use `and then` when the right side is only safe or useful if the left side is `True`. With a plain `and`, Ada may check both sides.

card: `if X > 0 then ... elsif ... else ... end if;`
`and then` / `or else` check the right side only when needed
`case N is when 1 | 2 => ... when others => ... end case;`

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with for loops over ranges, count down with reverse, and use while loops and exit when.

lesson.md: A `for` loop repeats code for every value in a range. In `for I in 1 .. 5 loop`, the loop variable `I` takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, one after the other. The loop ends with `end loop;`. You do not declare `I`: it exists only inside the loop, and you cannot change it.
With `reverse`, the loop counts down. The range itself is still written from small to large. A range like `5 .. 1` is empty, so its loop runs zero times.
A common pattern: declare a variable before the loop and update it in every round. Here `Sum` collects the numbers from 1 to 10.
A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is `True`. Ada checks the condition before every round. Use it when you do not know in advance how many rounds you need.

A plain `loop ... end loop;` repeats forever, unless `exit when condition;` stops it. The `exit when` line can be anywhere inside the loop. When its condition is `True`, the program continues after `end loop;`.
A `while` loop whose condition never becomes `False` runs forever. Make sure that something inside the loop changes the condition.

card: `for I in 1 .. 5 loop ... end loop;` counts up
`for I in reverse 1 .. 5 loop` counts down
`while N < 10 loop ... end loop;` repeats while `True`
`loop ... exit when Done; ... end loop;` stops anywhere

units.title: Procedures and functions
units.summary: Group code into procedures and functions, pass parameters with the modes in, out and in out, and return results.

lesson.md: A **procedure** is a named group of statements. You declare it inside `Main`, between `is` and `begin`, like a variable. Then you **call** it by writing its name as a statement. Procedures and functions together are called **subprograms**.
**Parameters** pass values into a subprogram. You list them in parentheses with name and type, like declarations. Several parameters are separated by `;` in the declaration and by `,` in the call.

lesson.output:
Hi, Ada
Hi, Ada
Hi, Bob

lesson.md: A **function** calculates a value and gives it back with `return`. Its declaration names the result type after the word `return`. You call a function inside an expression, wherever you need its value. `A, B : Integer` declares two parameters of the same type.

Every parameter has a **mode**. `in` is the default: the subprogram can only read the value. With `out`, the procedure writes a result into the variable of the caller. With `in out`, it reads the value and can change it. For `out` and `in out` the caller must pass a variable, not a fixed value like `7`.
An `in` parameter is read-only. A statement like `Total := 0;` inside `Split` does not compile.
Declare a subprogram before the code that calls it. The `end` of a subprogram repeats its name, for example `end Greet;`, so you always see what ends there.

card: `procedure Greet (Name : String) is begin ... end Greet;`
`function Square (X : Integer) return Integer is ...`
`return X * X;` gives the result back
`in` reads, `out` writes, `in out` reads and changes

units.title: Arrays
units.summary: Store many values in arrays, use 'First, 'Last, 'Length and 'Range, and loop over every element.

lesson.md: An **array** holds many values of the same type. Each value (an **element**) has a number, its **index**. In Ada, you first declare an array type, for example `type Scores is array (1 .. 3) of Integer;`. Then you declare variables of that type.

`(10, 20, 30)` is an **aggregate**: it lists a value for every element. You read or change one element with its index in parentheses, as in `S (2)`. The index starts where the range of the type starts, here at 1.

`'First` gives the first index, `'Last` the last index and `'Length` the number of elements. The aggregate `(others => 0)` sets every element to `0`. The range of an array does not have to start at 1.
`P'Range` means `P'First .. P'Last`, so `for I in P'Range loop` visits every index. If you only need the values, `for X of P loop` gives you each element directly.
An aggregate can also name indexes with `=>`. `(2 => 7, 4 => 9, others => 0)` sets element 2 to `7`, element 4 to `9` and all other elements to `0`.
A `String` is an array of characters with indexes starting at 1. A single **character** is written in single quotes, like `'-'`. `Put` can print one character.
An index outside the range stops the program with `Constraint_Error`. With the type `Scores` above, `S (4)` or `S (0)` is an error. Ada checks every index for you.

card: `type Row is array (1 .. 5) of Integer;` declares an array type
`R : Row := (others => 0);` fills every element
`R (2) := 7;` reads or writes one element
`R'First`, `R'Last`, `R'Length`, `R'Range`
`for X of R loop` visits every element

units.title: Your own types
units.summary: Create range types, enumerations and subtypes so that Ada finds mistakes for you.

lesson.md: In Ada, you create your own types to describe your data. A **range type** is a whole number type with limits: `type Percent is range 0 .. 100;`. A variable of this type can only hold values from 0 to 100.

Two different types never mix, even if both hold numbers. `A + O` with the types below does not compile, so you cannot add apples to oranges by mistake. If you really want to, convert both values to `Integer`. The `_` in `1_000` only makes the number easier to read.

An **enumeration** type lists all its values by name: `type Day is (Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun);`. `'Image` gives the name in capitals. `'Succ` gives the next value, `'Pred` the previous one, and `'Pos` the position, counted from 0.
`for L in Light loop` visits every value of the type. A `case` on an enumeration can list all values, so it needs no `when others`.

A **subtype** limits an existing type but stays compatible with it: `subtype Weekday is Day range Mon .. Fri;`. Ada has two useful subtypes of `Integer`: `Natural` (0 and up) and `Positive` (1 and up). You can mix a subtype with its type freely.
Ada checks the limits when the program runs. `Battery := 101;` or `Count := -1;` with a `Natural` stops the program with `Constraint_Error`. This finds mistakes early instead of storing wrong values.

card: `type Percent is range 0 .. 100;` a new number type
`type Color is (Red, Green, Blue);` an enumeration
`subtype Small is Integer range 1 .. 9;` limits a type
`Natural` is 0 and up, `Positive` is 1 and up
`Color'Succ (Red)`, `Color'Pos (Blue)`, `for C in Color loop`

units.title: Records
units.summary: Group related values into records, create them with aggregates, and keep records in arrays.

lesson.md: A **record** groups several values, which may have different types, under one name. Each part is a **component**. You declare a record type between `record` and `end record;`, and reach a component with a dot, as in `P.X`.

An aggregate sets all components at once. In a **named** aggregate like `(Name => "Ada", Age => 36)` you write each component name with `=>`. In a **positional** aggregate like `("Bob", 41)` the values follow the order of the components. A string component needs a fixed length, for example `String (1 .. 3)` for exactly 3 characters.
A component can have a default value in the type. `B := A;` copies all components, so later changes to `B` do not change `A`. `A = B` compares all components.
Arrays can hold records. `C (2).Price` reads the component `Price` of element 2. In `for It of C loop`, each `It` is a whole record.
Records work well as parameters. With `in out`, a procedure can change components of the record that the caller passes.
A component of type `String (1 .. 5)` holds exactly 5 characters. `"Pear"` has only 4, so it does not fit and Ada reports an error. Fill up with spaces, like `"Pear "`.

card: `type Point is record X, Y : Integer; end record;`
`P.X := 3;` reads or writes a component
